subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffee and the Enlightenment
description: A quick, practical guide to Coffee and the Enlightenment.

hook.text: Before coffee, Europe's daily drink was beer. Breakfast, lunch, dinner—always beer.

buildup.text: Coffee replaced morning alcohol with morning alertness. Historians call it a 'cognitive revolution.'

discovery.text: Voltaire drank 40–50 cups a day. Enlightenment thinkers fueled their ideas with caffeine, not alcohol.

twist.text: The French Revolution was partly planned in Paris coffeehouses. Camille Desmoulins rallied crowds from one.

climax.text: Coffee didn't cause the Enlightenment, but it gave thinkers a sober, social place to sharpen ideas.

punchline.text: Europe sobered up and started thinking. Coffee helped.

quiz.question: What drink did coffee largely replace in Europe's daily routine?

details.summary: Coffee arrived in Europe as the Enlightenment was dawning. Coffeehouses became meeting places for scientists, philosophers, and writers. Coffee replaced alcohol as the drink of intellectual work, sharpening debate instead of dulling it.
details.whyItMatters: The claim that coffee fueled the Enlightenment is debatable but thought-provoking. The shift from a beer-based to a coffee-based society genuinely transformed European intellectual productivity.
takeaways: Coffee arrived in Europe as the Enlightenment was beginning
It replaced alcohol as the intellectual beverage of choice
Coffeehouses became hubs for scientific and philosophical debate

faq.question: Did coffee actually cause the Enlightenment?
faq.answer: That is an oversimplification, but the connection is real. Before coffee, Europeans drank beer and wine throughout the day. Coffee replaced morning alcohol, producing an alert population. Coffeehouses provided sober gathering places for debate. This combination contributed to intellectual ferment.

faq.question: Which Enlightenment thinkers frequented coffeehouses?
faq.answer: Voltaire reportedly drank 50 cups a day at Cafe Procope. Montesquieu, Diderot, and other Encyclopedists worked in Parisian cafes. In London, scientists like Newton and Halley frequented coffeehouses near the Royal Society. The list of coffeehouse intellectuals spans every field.
